subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla

subjective.question: Differentiate between arthropods and annelids.
subjective.answer: Arthropods are invertebrate animals that possess a segmented body, an exoskeleton, and paired jointed appendages, whereas annelids are segmented worms marked by transverse rings. Arthropods have an exoskeleton but annelids do not. Arthropods have an open circulatory system while annelids have a closed circulatory system. Arthropods have a chitinous cuticle while annelids have a collagenous cuticle. Insects, crustaceans and arachnids are groups of arthropods, while earthworms, ragworms and leeches are groups of annelids.

subjective.question: Describe the body wall of a turbellarian.
subjective.answer: A basement membrane separates the epidermis from the mesodermally derived tissues. An outer layer of circular muscles and an inner layer of longitudinal muscles lie beneath the basement membrane. The innermost layer is the endodermis (gastrodermis) that lines the digestive cavity. Rhabdites form a protective mucus sheath around the body, possibly in response to attempted predation or desiccation. Adhesive glands attach the turbellarian to the substrate, and releaser glands release an enzyme that dissolves the attachment. Turbellarians move using cilia and muscular undulation. Most are carnivores, some are herbivores, and digestion is both extracellular and intracellular.

subjective.question: Differentiate between monoecious and dioecious species.
subjective.answer: In monoecious species, a single individual produces both male and female reproductive structures (both sexes are present in the same individual). In dioecious species, individuals are either male or female: each individual, when it produces reproductive structures, produces only male or only female structures.

subjective.question: What is the function of the pellicle in protozoa?
subjective.answer: Most protozoans are enclosed by a skeletal structure known as the pellicle, consisting of the plasma membrane and the underlying cytoskeleton (with additional membranes, microtubules, microfilaments, or plates of cellulose or protein). The pellicle maintains the shape of the cell.

subjective.question: Define typhlosole.
subjective.answer: A typhlosole is a dorsal (longitudinal) fold of the intestinal wall (luminal epithelium) that substantially increases the surface area of the intestine for absorption and digestion. Typhlosoles occur in bivalve molluscs, some annelids and some echinoderms.

subjective.question: What is the tubular system in nematodes?
subjective.answer: Parasitic nematodes have a more advanced excretory system called the tubular system, which developed from the renette system. In this system, the renettes unite to form a large canal which opens to the outside through an excretory pore.

subjective.question: List the characteristics of phylum Cnidaria.
subjective.answer: 1. Radial or biradial symmetry. 2. Diploblastic, tissue-level organization. 3. A gastrovascular cavity. 4. Gelatinous mesoglea between the epidermal and gastrodermal tissue layers. 5. Nervous system in the form of a nerve net. 6. Specialized cells called cnidocytes, used in defense, feeding and attachment. 7. No circulatory system; exchange occurs by cellular diffusion and through the mesoglea. 8. A ciliated planula larva is found. (Cnidaria: Gr. knide, nettle.)

subjective.question: Give the characteristics of deuterostomes.
subjective.answer: Deuterostomes are also known as enterocoelomates because their coelom forms through enterocoely, and in them the blastopore typically becomes the anus while the mouth forms separately. There are three major clades of deuterostomes: 1. Chordata (vertebrates and their kin), 2. Echinodermata (starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers, etc.), and 3. Hemichordata (acorn worms and graptolites). Deuterostomia is a sister clade of Protostomia, and together they form the Nephrozoa clade.

subjective.question: What evolutionary adaptations do parasitic nematodes show?
subjective.answer: Parasitic nematodes show a number of evolutionary adaptations to their way of life: 1. They have high reproductive potential. 2. Their life cycles increase the likelihood of transmission from one host to another. 3. They develop an enzyme-resistant cuticle, resistant eggs, and encysted larvae.

subjective.question: Differentiate between monophyletic, diphyletic and polyphyletic groups.
subjective.answer: A monophyletic group includes a single ancestral species and all of its descendants; such a group is also called a clade, and arranging animals into monophyletic groups is the goal of animal systematics. A diphyletic origin means the group is derived from two ancestors; some zoologists believe the animal kingdom is at least diphyletic, with the Porifera derived separately from all other phyla — the similarity of poriferan choanocytes and choanoflagellate protists suggests evolutionary ties between these groups. A polyphyletic group has members that can be traced to several separate ancestors and lacks a single common ancestor, so it is an unnatural assemblage that is normally reclassified when recognized.

subjective.question: What is a spongocoel?
subjective.answer: Ostia are the outer openings of porocytes and lead directly to a chamber called the spongocoel. It is a single, large, spacious central cavity in the sponge's body. The asconoid body form, in which the spongocoel opens directly through the osculum, is the simplest and least common sponge body form.

subjective.question: Define determinate cleavage.
subjective.answer: Determinate cleavage is a characteristic common to many protostomes in which early cleavage is determinate, meaning that the fate of the cells is established very early in development — each blastomere's developmental fate is set at the first divisions.

subjective.question: Describe the circulatory system of cephalopods.
subjective.answer: Cephalopods have a closed circulatory system: blood is confined to vessels throughout its circuit around the body, and capillary beds connect arteries and veins, across which gases, nutrients and metabolic wastes are exchanged. In addition to a systemic heart consisting of two auricles and one ventricle, cephalopods have contractile arteries and structures called branchial (gill) hearts at the base of each gill, which help move blood through the gills. These modifications increase blood pressure and the rate of blood flow, necessary for active animals with relatively high metabolic rates. Cephalopods use hemocyanin, a copper-containing protein, to transport oxygen, so their blood is colorless when deoxygenated and blue when oxygenated. The closed system also gives them greater excretory efficiency.

subjective.question: What is the role of osphradia in molluscs?
subjective.answer: Osphradia are chemoreceptors located in the anterior wall of the mantle cavity, near the gill, connected with one of the visceral ganglia. They detect sediment and chemicals in the inhalant water (testing the purity of the water passing to the gills), and in predatory gastropods they help detect prey.

subjective.question: Define a siphon in molluscs.
subjective.answer: Some gastropods and other molluscs have a rolled extension of the mantle, called a siphon, that serves as an inhalant tube. Siphons are tube-like structures in which water (or, rarely, air) flows; the water flow is used for locomotion, feeding, respiration and reproduction, and is directed to or from the mantle cavity.

subjective.question: Give a general account of phylum Nematoda.
subjective.answer: Phylum Nematoda is a phylum of invertebrate animals comprising the roundworms (nematodes). They are identifiable by their smooth, tough outer cuticle and narrow, cylindrical, unsegmented body; their name is derived from the Greek word nema (nematos), meaning 'thread'. They are pseudocoelomates, possess a complete digestive system, and shed their cuticle in order to grow (ecdysis). Soil nematodes feed on bacteria, fungi and other nematodes and play an important role in nutrient recycling, while many species are parasites of plants and animals.

subjective.question: Define ecdysis and describe its four stages.
subjective.answer: Ecdysis is the process of an arthropod moulting its exoskeleton; growth would be virtually impossible unless the exoskeleton were periodically shed. Its four stages are: (1) Enzymes secreted from hypodermal glands begin digesting the old procuticle, separating the hypodermis from the exoskeleton (apolysis), and the molting fluid digests and absorbs the old endocuticle. (2) A new procuticle and epicuticle are secreted. (3) The old exoskeleton splits open along predetermined ecdysial lines when the animal stretches by air or water intake; pores in the procuticle secrete additional epicuticle. (4) Finally, calcium carbonate deposits and/or sclerotization harden the new exoskeleton.

subjective.question: What is the schizocoel hypothesis about the origin of the coelom?
subjective.answer: According to the schizocoel hypothesis, the coelom is formed by the splitting of the mesoderm, as in protostomes. It suggests that a triploblastic acoelomate (flatworm-like) body form is the ancestor of the coelomate body plan.

subjective.question: What is heartworm disease?
subjective.answer: Heartworm disease is a serious disease that results in severe lung disease, heart failure, other organ damage, and death in pets, mainly dogs, cats and ferrets. It is caused by a parasitic worm called Dirofilaria immitis, and the worms are spread through the bite of a mosquito.

subjective.question: What is the mastax in rotifers?
subjective.answer: The pharynx of rotifers contains a structure called the mastax (jaws). The mastax is a muscular organ that grinds food. Its inner walls contain several sets of hard jaws called trophi, which have different structures in different species.

subjective.question: How does Hydra reproduce?
subjective.answer: The common asexual method of reproduction in hydras is budding. Buds originate at the junction of the stalk and gastric regions; a bud begins as a hemispherical outpouching that eventually elongates, becomes cylindrical, and develops tentacles. The bud then pinches off and a new independent individual is formed. Hydra also reproduces sexually by the fusion of gametes, generally when environmental conditions become unfavorable (in autumn).

subjective.question: How do oligochaete worms mate?
subjective.answer: To mate, oligochaete worms lie next to each other, head to tail, so that the clitellum of one worm aligns with the sexual organs (seminal receptacles) of the other. Both worms exchange sperm with each other, and the received sperm is held by the recipient in its seminal receptacles until the eggs are ready to be fertilized.

subjective.question: What are pinacocytes in phylum Porifera?
subjective.answer: Pinacocytes are one of the three types of cells found in phylum Porifera. They are thin, flat cells that line the outer surface of the sponge, forming the pinacoderm.

subjective.question: What is trichinosis?
subjective.answer: Trichinosis is a food-borne disease caused by a microscopic parasitic nematode called Trichinella. People get this disease by eating raw or undercooked meat from infected animals. The young larvae encyst in the skeletal muscles and remain infective for many years.

subjective.question: What is the common character of arthropods and nematodes?
subjective.answer: The nematodes and the arthropods belong to a clade with a common ancestor, called Ecdysozoa. The name comes from the word ecdysis, which refers to the periodic shedding, or molting, of the exoskeleton (cuticle).

subjective.question: What is pinocytosis?
subjective.answer: Pinocytosis is the process in which food is engulfed (taken in) in the form of liquid — the cell takes in droplets of fluid containing dissolved food material.

subjective.question: Write down the characteristics of phylum Arthropoda.
subjective.answer: 1. They have paired, jointed appendages. 2. Ecdysis or molting takes place during growth. 3. They have a ventral nervous system. 4. The coelom is reduced to cavities around the gonads and sometimes the excretory organs, the main body cavity being a hemocoel. 5. They possess a chitinous exoskeleton and a segmented body divided into specialized regions (tagmata).

subjective.question: Write a short note on rotifers.
subjective.answer: Rotifers are microscopic pseudocoelomate animals abundant in most freshwater habitats; a few species (less than 10%) are marine. Some have beautiful colors, although most are transparent, and some have odd and bizarre shapes. They are triploblastic, bilateral, unsegmented and pseudocoelomate. Their pharynx contains a mastax with trophi (jaws) that grinds food, and the ciliated corona creates water currents for feeding and locomotion.

subjective.question: Describe the excretory system of the earthworm.
subjective.answer: Excretion in the earthworm is performed by long, thin, coiled tubules known as nephridia, found in all segments except the first two. Each nephridium is a small microscopic coiled tube with a thin, glandular and vascular wall. According to location, nephridia are of three types: septal nephridia, pharyngeal nephridia and integumentary nephridia.

subjective.question: Differentiate between protonephridia and metanephridia.
subjective.answer: Protonephridia are tubular excretory structures in certain invertebrates (e.g., flatworms) that form a network of dead-end tubules without internal openings, ending internally in flame cells and opening outside through a pore. Metanephridia are the primitive excretory organs present in many invertebrates (e.g., annelids), composed of a ciliated funnel-like opening (nephrostome) that opens into the coelom and conducts wastes to the outside.

subjective.question: Differentiate between polyp and medusa.
subjective.answer: The polyp is a sessile life-cycle stage of phylum Cnidaria (e.g., sea anemones and adult corals): it has a mouth surrounded by tentacles facing upward toward the water, and is attached to the bottom by a foot-like disk; it reproduces either sexually or asexually. The medusa is the free-swimming stage (e.g., jellyfish of class Hydrozoa and others): it is bell-shaped and can undergo muscular contractions that enable it to swim, with tentacles, photoreceptors and gravity-sensing statocysts around the bell; it reproduces sexually.

subjective.question: What are the advantages of a coelom?
subjective.answer: A true coelom provides space in which organs such as the digestive tract can grow, and organs such as the gonads that need more space only during the breeding season can expand. The coelomic fluid acts as a hydrostatic skeleton and as a circulatory medium for transporting food, wastes and gases, and the coelom allows the formation of well-organized organ systems and greater body flexibility and movement independent of the gut.

subjective.question: How is the coelom formed in protostomes and deuterostomes?
subjective.answer: In protostomes, the coelom forms when the mesoderm splits through the process of schizocoely, while in deuterostomes the coelom forms when the mesoderm pinches off through the process of enterocoely. Protostomes undergo spiral cleavage, while deuterostomes undergo radial cleavage. The fate of the blastopore also differs: in protostomes it becomes the mouth, whereas in deuterostomes the mouth forms separately and the blastopore often becomes the anus.

subjective.question: Name the species of Plasmodium that cause malaria in humans.
subjective.answer: Five species of Plasmodium (single-celled parasites) can infect humans and cause malaria: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium malariae, Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium ovale and Plasmodium knowlesi.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Explain the skeleton of a sea urchin.
subjective.answer: Sea urchins are rounded, and their oral end is oriented toward the substrate. Their skeleton, called a test, consists of 10 closely fitting plates that arch between the oral and aboral ends. Five rows of ambulacral plates have openings for tube feet and alternate with five interambulacral plates, which have tubercles for the articulation of spines. The base of each spine is a concave socket, and muscles at its base move the spine. Spines are often sharp, sometimes hollow, and may contain venom dangerous to swimmers.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What are garden centipedes?
subjective.answer: Members of the class Symphyla are small arthropods (2 to 10 mm in length) that occupy soil and leaf mold, superficially resemble centipedes, and are often called garden centipedes. (Symphyla: Gr. sym, same; phyllos, leaf.)

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Describe the circulatory system of insects.
subjective.answer: The circulatory system of insects is similar to that described for other arthropods, although the blood vessels are less well developed. Insects, like all other arthropods, have an open circulatory system, which differs in both structure and function from the closed circulatory system found in humans and other vertebrates. In a closed system, blood is always contained within vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries, or the heart itself); in the open system of insects, the blood (hemolymph) flows freely in the body cavity (hemocoel) for much of its circuit.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: How do insects pollinate plants?
subjective.answer: Insects are responsible for the pollination of approximately 65% of all plant species. Insects and flowering plants have co-evolutionary relationships that directly benefit humans; the annual value of insect-pollinated crops is estimated at $19 billion per year in the United States. Insect pollination is as simple as insects like bees, butterflies and wasps flying from flower to flower to collect nectar; in the process, pollen collects on their bodies and rubs off on the other flowers they visit.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Describe the ventilating process in insects.
subjective.answer: Most insects have ventilating mechanisms that move air into and out of the tracheal system. Insects do not breathe through their mouths and do not have lungs; their blood does not carry oxygen and carbon dioxide. Instead, they have a system of tubes, called tracheae, that penetrate right through the body. Air enters the tracheae by pores called spiracles, found on each side of the abdomen, each segment having a pair of spiracles. As oxygen diffuses from the tracheae to the body tissues and is not replaced by carbon dioxide, a vacuum is created that draws more air into the spiracles; this process is called passive suction.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Describe the stomach of a starfish.
subjective.answer: The mouth opens into a short esophagus and then into a large stomach that fills most of the coelom of the central disk. The stomach is divided into two regions: the larger, oral stomach, sometimes called the cardiac stomach, receives ingested food and can be pushed out of the mouth to engulf prey; it joins the smaller, aboral stomach, sometimes called the pyloric stomach, where digestion continues.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What is complete metamorphosis?
subjective.answer: Complete metamorphosis is the type of insect development that includes four stages — egg, larva, pupa and adult — which differ greatly in morphology. Butterflies, ants, fleas, bees, beetles, moths and wasps are examples of complete metamorphosis.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What are the classes of hormones in insects?
subjective.answer: There are two main classes of hormones in insects: 1. The true hormones produced by epithelial glands, belonging to the ecdysteroids (molting hormones) or juvenile hormones. 2. The neuropeptide hormones produced by neurosecretory cells.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Describe the nervous system of insects.
subjective.answer: The central nervous system consists of a series of ganglia that supply nerves to successive segments of the body. The three main ganglia in the head (protocerebrum, deutocerebrum and tritocerebrum) are commonly fused to form the brain. The rest of the ganglionic chain lies below the alimentary canal against the ventral body surface. In most insects the number of separate ganglia has been reduced by fusion; the last abdominal ganglion always serves several segments, and in homopterans and heteropterans all the abdominal ganglia usually fuse with the mesothoracic and metathoracic ganglia.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Give the general features of class Crinoidea.
subjective.answer: Members of class Crinoidea (sea lilies and feather stars) have a stem and a crown consisting of a cup-like central body known as the theca, with five rays or arms. The mouth is surrounded by feeding arms and is linked to a U-shaped gut. They are passive suspension feeders. They are dioecious, and the gonads are located in the pinnules, or in a few cases in the arms. Sea lilies attach permanently to their substrate by a stalk; the unattached end of a sea lily is called the crown.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What are ossicles?
subjective.answer: The echinoderm skeleton consists of a series of calcium carbonate plates called ossicles. In sea stars these form a series of overlapping skeletal plates in the body wall that give support while retaining flexibility.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What are alarm pheromones?
subjective.answer: Alarm pheromones are pheromones released to warn other individuals of danger. They may cause orientation toward the pheromone source and elicit a subsequent attack or flight from the source.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Do insects have memory?
subjective.answer: Research has demonstrated that insects are capable of some learning and have a memory. For example, bees (order Hymenoptera) instinctively recognize flower-like objects by their shape and ability to absorb ultraviolet light, which makes the center of the flower appear dark. Insects acquire more than one type of spatial memory, acquire these memories at different rates, and change which memories they use as they become more familiar with an environment.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: How do sea stars regenerate?
subjective.answer: Sea stars are well known for their powers of regeneration. They can regenerate any part of a broken arm. In a few species, an entire sea star can be regenerated from a broken arm if the arm contains a portion of the central disk. Regeneration is a slow process, taking up to a year for complete regeneration.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What are pheromones?
subjective.answer: Pheromones are chemicals an animal releases that cause behavioral or physiological changes in another member of the same species. Zoologists have described many different insect uses of pheromones, including sex attractants, alarm pheromones and trail pheromones; the pheromone that the queen releases controls the honeybee caste system.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Define a vector.
subjective.answer: A vector is a living organism that transmits an infectious agent from an infected animal to a human or another animal. Vectors are frequently arthropods, such as mosquitoes, ticks, flies, fleas and lice.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What is royal jelly?
subjective.answer: Royal jelly is a honey bee secretion used in the nutrition of larvae, as well as of adult queens. It is secreted from the glands in the hypopharynx of nurse bees and fed to all larvae in the colony, regardless of sex or caste.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: How does gaseous exchange occur in ophiuroids?
subjective.answer: In ophiuroids (brittle stars), gaseous exchange takes place through ten bursae (sacs) on the oral side of the central disk. Cilia within the sacs direct water flow so that oxygen can be absorbed from the water; water flows through the action of cilia or muscular contraction, and oxygen is transported by the hemal system.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What is paurometabolous metamorphosis?
subjective.answer: Paurometabolous metamorphosis is the process of gradual (incomplete) metamorphosis. It is the type of growth that occurs in insects such as cockroaches and grasshoppers, which includes just three stages — egg, nymph and adult. It is called incomplete metamorphosis because it lacks the pupa stage; the immature stages are called nymphs.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What is Aristotle's lantern?
subjective.answer: Aristotle's lantern is the chewing apparatus of sea urchins (echinoids), a conical-shaped structure that can be projected from the mouth. It is a complex arrangement of muscles and calcareous teeth constituting about 35 ossicles (with five strong teeth), used for masticating food. The teeth are extruded to scrape algae and other food from rocks; echinoids feed on algae, bryozoans, coral polyps and dead animal remains.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Give the characteristic features of class Asteroidea.
subjective.answer: Class Asteroidea (sea stars) has about 1,900 species and is the second largest group in the Echinodermata. They often live on hard substrates in marine environments. Thin folds of the body wall, called dermal branchiae, serve in gas exchange, and pincher-like structures called pedicellariae are present. There is an ambulacral groove with paired rows of tube feet, and suction disks and sensory receptors are distributed over the surface of the body and tube feet. Sea stars are dioecious, external fertilization is the rule, and the larva is the bipinnaria larva.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What is the hemal system of echinoderms?
subjective.answer: In echinoderms, the blood vascular system is called the hemal system. It is poorly developed in starfish and plays little role in circulation. The system consists of small fluid-filled sinus channels that lack a distinct lining; the hemal channels are actually intercommunicating spaces and are not true blood vessels.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What are dermal branchiae?
subjective.answer: Dermal branchiae (papulae) are external gill-like structures — thin folds of the body wall — scattered across the body surface of sea stars. They function in gas exchange: cilia beat and ventilate the respiratory surface, and the papulae act as a simple site of respiratory exchange. They consist of an outer ectodermal epithelium, gland cells and a small basiepithelial nerve plexus.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: How do sea cucumbers move?
subjective.answer: Sea cucumbers are mostly sluggish burrowers and creepers, although some swim by undulating their bodies from side to side. Locomotion using tube feet is inefficient because the tube feet are not anchored by body-wall ossicles; locomotion more commonly results from contractions of body-wall muscles that produce wormlike locomotor waves passing along the length of the body. To confuse or harm predators, sea cucumbers can propel their own toxic internal organs (Cuverian tubules of the respiratory tree) toward an attacker; the organs grow back.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What is synchronous (direct) flight in insects?
subjective.answer: Direct or synchronous flight is a mode of flight fueled by wing muscles that insert directly into the wing base. The insertion point of the wing is hinged, which enables the downward movements of the muscles to lift the wing portion upward, and upward movements to pull the wing portion downward.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: How do cycliophores reproduce asexually?
subjective.answer: Cycliophores can reproduce asexually by producing a larval stage, called the Pandora larva, that is released and settles on the same host. Because of this asexual reproduction, a large number of symbion (Symbion pandora) can build up on one host.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Differentiate between sea lilies and feather stars.
subjective.answer: Sea lilies have a stalk below the crown and look like flowers; they are mostly white, live in deep water, and attach permanently to the substrate by the stalk. Feather stars have a cluster of tentacles (cirri) below the crown and look like ferns; they are white, purple, brown, green or violet, and most live on coral reefs. Both are plankton feeders (passive suspension feeders).

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: What is trepang?
subjective.answer: The body wall of sea cucumbers, when boiled and dried, is known as trepang in Asian countries, where it is used as food.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Which animals belong to class Diplopoda?
subjective.answer: Members of the class Diplopoda are the millipedes. Most millipedes are slow-moving detritivores, eating decaying leaves and other dead plant matter.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Describe the mating behavior of insects.
subjective.answer: Mating behavior typically comprises all events from pair formation through courtship to the final breakup of the mating pair. Most insects have complex mating behaviors for locating and recognizing a potential mate, for positioning a mate for copulation, or for pacifying an aggressive mate. Locating and recognizing mates may involve chemical attractants (pheromones, e.g., moths, order Lepidoptera), visual signals (fireflies, order Coleoptera), and auditory signals (cicadas, order Homoptera; grasshoppers, crickets and katydids, order Orthoptera). Copulation is usually by internal fertilization, through insertion of the male intromittent organ into the female genital tract for deposition of sperm.

subjective.topic: Current Paper Questions — Insects, Echinoderms and Minor Phyla
subjective.question: Why are soil-dwelling insects important?
subjective.answer: Soil-dwelling insects play important roles in aeration, drainage and turnover of soil, and they promote decay processes. Other insects serve important roles in food webs. Soil-dwelling insects are hidden in the soil and hard to detect until the sudden appearance of damage creates the demand for rapid, curative treatment.
